caption:
When you think you came in dead last but end up top 15% women and top 20% overall in the 50k at Canada’s largest trail race 🙈 Soo grateful that my body held up and survived all the type 2 fun stories that came with it 😜 

From numerous water crossings to running up and down 50% grade mountains and ridges, legs cramping up because it was SO hot and talking myself out of quitting, making friends on trail, and only remembering to press record when I was walking… this is my attempt to bring you along every hour of the race so enjoy! 🫶 

Watch to the end to see how bad my tan got 🙈

Would you ever run a @sinister_sports Sinister 7 trail race? 

___ 

If you’re new here welcome, I’m Candace your new outdoorsy bestie! Follow @ajourneyinspired for more trail running adventures and tips ☺️

This weekend, Geoff and I ran the infamous Squamish 50 together! If you’ve been here for a while, thank you for following along with training updates.  It’s been so special to bring you on this journey to one of the most iconic ultra races in Canada ❤️

Squam is known as one of the hardest 50ks in the country because
⛰️ it has a crazy elevation profile (2500m/8500ft up + 2750m/9000ft down which sounds easier than it is in reality)
🚫 No poles are allowed!
⏳Short 11.5h cutoff
🌲 Extremely technical trails full of roots, rocks, and descents. Quite a bit of scrambling required and some parts weren’t runnable

🌧️ An atmospheric river was forecast all weekend so the trails were slippery. Somehow we lucked out with perfect weather on race day so I can’t complain 😍

On top of that, scoliosis brought me new challenges, and Geoff raced with not one but two sprained ankles.

Life didn’t slow down either. I worked full-time in finance, Geoff in tech, both of us juggling side projects, sports (Geoff with hockey and soccer), bucket list trips, and being there for family across the country. Training wasn’t about having free time… it was about making it fit.

Things that worked for us / we’re grateful for:
🥤 Dialing in race-day nutrition with a sports dietitian was game changer 
👟 Finding our perfect trail shoes - the @merrellcanada Agility Peak 5
🙌 Support from our friends @leanna__b and Milo. We usually run self-supported, so this felt incredible (and Lenka got us footage we’ve never had before!).
💦 @hydrapak’s gear and support as always! 

Crossing that finish line proved that first ultras don’t need perfect circumstances. The course is hard, the training takes commitment, but it’s possible to fit it alongside real life.

If we (two very normal people) can do this, so can you. We hope this inspires you!

Trail running Part 2: Let’s talk about what I packed for a trail ultramarathon in the Rockies! 

If you’re one of those people who are getting sucked into the ultramarathon / endurance running algorithm🤭, I hope this helps! I’ll be sharing more in my trail running series so follow along :) 

Don’t let the “short” distance of a 50k fool you. It’s not like running a road marathon and adding 10k 🥲 If you’re running a race like Sinister 7 there are lots of things to consider to keep you safe in the backcountry. Even having to camp the night before adds a ton to the packing list! it’s not uncommon to DNF this race even if it’s not the 50 or 100 miler because the race of any distance is gruelling and the trail is unforgiving. I hear stories of people injuring themselves and having to call SAR during this race so it’s always better to be safe than sorry. 

So without further ado, here’s what I packed in my ultralight @ospreypacks Dyna Pro 7 vest (full disclosure: I got this vest to do UGC work for osprey and absolutely love it!) 

- @blackdiamond distance carbon z poles 
- first aid kit and emergency blanket 
- headlamp 
- @garmincanada in reach 
- timing chip (not sure why people wore it on their ankles like a house arrest monitor)
- first 4 hours of carbs @digdeepef @paolabsjelly @humagel @naakbars (stay tuned for my post on what I ate for 8 hours)
- @saltstick tabs (spoiler: I had to call in backup salt during the race because it was SO HOT) 
- last 4 hours of carbs went into the bag that my crew (brother) gave me at the halfway point 
- @suniienergygum caffeine gum 
- @hydrapak flasks x 3 
- water filter 

Not shown: 
- race clothes (check out the tags in my previous post) 
- bib 
- extra socks (so. Many. water crossings 🥵) 
- left behind the bear spray (in grizzly country🫣!) -  the extra weight wasn’t necessary when there were lots of people on trail 

Any questions about trail running? Let me know in the comments :) I’ll be sharing more about what I ate and nutrition plan next!

Went to Colombia to hike and learn Spanish, ended up finding out our favourite activity there is outdoor climbing!

I know I know… you’re probably shocked that we haven’t done this before because we have easy access to Squamish, but to be fair, we’ve only lived in Vancouver for officially less than 2 years 🙈 

As soon as we discovered this hidden gem activity in Suesca Colombia, we had to try it. Suesca was the birthplace of rock climbing in Colombia and known as one of the best places to climb in South America, with over 500 routes for trad, sport and bouldering styles. 

Our guide Juan was phenomenal. He was so patient and attentive to our needs and made us feel completely safe. And if you’re a good climber already, it takes a local like him to navigate these sandstone mountains. 

This side quest is much more affordable than you can find in Canada too. At only $90usd pp we got a private guide, gear rentals, food, and a full day of climbing. 

I think we may have caught the climbing bug after this experience. We’d highly recommend that you 📌 save this and put outdoor rock climbing in Colombia on your bucketlist. 

So if you’re craving a side quest, go to @suescalada_com and make sure you ask for Juan, you’ll have the best time ever!

caption:
HOW TO GO WHALE WATCHING IN VANCOUVER (FOR FREE) 🐋⬇️

How lucky are we to live in a place like this? 🥹 Yesterday I ran 6km to the ocean and back home just to watch whales swim by at sunset. I had this little spot almost entirely to myself, and it felt so magical.

One of my favourite things about whale watching is the people it brings together. Over two days of waiting for whales, I ended up making two new friends that I still keep in touch with.

Ever since I shared this sighting on my story yesterday, I’ve been getting so many questions about how to see whales in Vancouver. While there’s definitely some luck involved, there are also ways to improve your chances.

Also, if you’ve been seeing whale videos all over social media lately, they’re real!! Whales are showing up in local waters more and more often. Humpbacks made a crazy comeback and Bigg’s orcas are spending more time in the Salish Sea because of ideal temperatures and food sources. 

I’m sharing this because the more we understand the wildlife around us the more we can help protect it. When people care about these animals, they’re more likely to support conservation efforts and give wildlife the space they need to thrive.

📌Save this post for my tips ⬇️

1. April through October is the prime window for whale watching, with July and August often offering the best conditions.
2. Join the “Howe Sound and Sea to Sky Wildlife Sightings” Facebook group.
3. Ask an admin to join their Discord group. It’s the fastest and most accurate way I’ve found to get whale updates.
4. I also used the Whale Locator app (There are many other resources online). It’s helpful for general areas, but Discord still is best. 
5. Watch for seabirds which indicate bait fish which can attract whales. 
6. bring binoculars and look for the blow especially in the morning and evening when it’s calmer.
7. Track whale watching boats 
8. If you’re on the water, always stay at least 200m away and give whales plenty of space.

These mountains, forests, rivers and coastlines weren’t waiting to be discovered. They have been cared for by Indigenous Peoples since forever, and every trail, lake and valley holds stories that began long before Canada did.

I don’t think celebrating Canada Day and reflecting on our history have to be at odds with one another. Actually, I think they belong together.

So today I’m feeling grateful for the privilege of exploring this land, for the people who continue to care for it, and for the opportunity to keep learning what it truly means to call this place home.

caption:
What happens when you challenge your friends to make ice cream by running 16km on one of Vancouver’s most well known trails? A lot of stares from strangers, laughter, blood and sweat, pretty views, and failures 😂

Out of 5, how many trail ice creams do you think worked? 🤭 

Here’s how we made the ice cream: 
1. Combine 1/2 cup heavy cream, 1/2 cup whole milk, flavour, and 1 tbsp sugar into a small freezer bag 
2. Submerge that small bag into a larger bag with 4 cups ice and 1/2 cup salt. The salt lowers the freezing point of the ice which makes the ice colder than normal. 

Tips: 
- you don’t need to run 16km for this to work! My ice cream was pretty much ready by 4km 
- squeeze out the air from your ice cream mixture bag because air acts as insulation and might prevent the cream from freezing 
- I chose a well padded running vest (@arcteryxbc norvan 14) so it would have less contact with my sweaty back 
- share ingredients with your friends bc you won’t need much per person. Thanks to @davidhui11 for organizing this, carrying the waffle cones, and making all of this happen! 

In the end, only Geoff and my ice creams (@traderjoes cookie butter and black sesame) worked. That was a 2/5 (40%) success rate and we couldn’t figure out why! The other ice creams remained liquid which was so sad 🥲

caption:
I decided to post something a little different today.🙃

I’ve been thinking about how Earth Day always brings a lot of conversation around caring for the planet, but also how easy it is to treat it like an annual reminder instead of something that should be a part of our everyday. 

The outdoors doesn’t really need a day of awareness. It needs quieter and more consistent choices from us when no one’s really watching every day. 

For example…taking a moment to understand whose land we’re on before we step onto it. Staying on trail even when it’s easier not to. Being a bit more thoughtful about geotagging and sharing locations widely on social media. Picking up what isn’t ours and leaving things a little better than we found them. And staying informed and supporting the people and groups doing the unglamorous work of protecting these spaces.

It’s not complicated but it does take thoughtfulness and intention. No one is perfect, but as a creator in the outdoor space I feel like I have the duty to talk about how we can be more intentional about our impact as we recreate in the places we care about.

All this to say, earth day isn’t just a reminder of the privilege we have … it’s a check in on what we’re choosing to do with the rest of the days, and I think there’s something comforting about that :)

BACKPACKING STARTER TIPS:

1️⃣Start with smaller hikes to build confidence on your feet:
- Get the free AllTrails app and filter for trails <5km near you, <100m gain, rated easy with 4+ stars
- Try finding trails that are maintained and have cell service
- Find a hiking community (there are plenty on Facebook)

2️⃣Try front country camping and learn survival skills from YouTube or a friend, including:
- Fire starting
- Tent pitching
- Water treatment
- Bear safety

3️⃣Start hiking longer and less-traveled trails in the mountains to increase fitness and gain path finding skills.
- Filter for a trail that’s 10km+ with >200m gain, rated moderate to hard
- Safety tips: Leave your info with a loved one, learn how to read a topo map, and carry a satellite device and paper map

4️⃣Backpack a short overnighter — choose a campsite that takes <3hours to hike to or are <10km one way on Alltrails.

5️⃣Stack new challenges with each adventure - winter backpacking is so fun!

caption:
RAIN JACKET 101 ☔️ if you think your jacket is broken because it stopped keeping you dry, it might just be dirty 👀

And I get it, these jackets are expensive, so it’s easy to feel disappointed when it stops working all of a sudden.

What’s actually happening is dirt, sweat, sunscreen, and body oils build up over time and block the fabric from being waterproof. Most of the time, it’s actually fixable!

Here’s what to do: (This applies to most waterproof hiking rain jackets or other gear, not just gore-tex)

1) use a tech wash. Don’t use a regular detergent which messes with the coating and no fabric softener at all because it’ll ruin performance
2) wash on a warm cycle and rinse it really well
3) low heat in the dryer if the care label allows it. This helps bring the waterproofing back
4) and if the jacket it still isn’t beading, that’s when you reapply a DWR spray or use a DWR detergent as an extra step before drying

I personally like @nikwaxna and @grangersofficial for rewaterproofing my outdoor gear.

💡 A few things I wish more people knew:
• Don’t wait until your jacket doesn’t work anymore! Regular light washes keep it performing for longer
• Spot clean your jacket if you get it dirty between wash cycles with dish detergent or a gentle stain remover like Eaze Out 
• Check cuffs, collar, and shoulders first. That’s where oils build up the most
• Always wash on its own or with one other Goretex item (not with towels or jeans or other laundry) so it doesn’t get beat up in the machine
• Follow the detergent bottle instructions closely, especially if you have a top load machine with an agitator. Some people tie a towel around the agitator so it doesn’t tear the delicate gear

And that’s how you make your rain jacket last years longer, keep things out of the landfill and save money. When was the last time you washed yours?

PS. I know it might feel like everyone has an Arc’teryx jacket but it really isn’t necessary. Let me know if you want recommendations for a more affordable one because I’ve tried many and have found some great ones at a fraction of the price! 

Save this, send it to a friend, and follow @ajourneyinspired for more outdoor gear tips! ☺️

caption:
If you’re tired of seeing the same hikes and the same travel destinations over and over, I was too. That’s how I ended up here. 

Most people visit Colombia for places like Medellín, Cartagena, or the Cocora Valley. Meanwhile, tucked away in the mountains is a national park that protects some of the country’s last glaciers and sees only a fraction of the visitors that other trekking destinations get.

The crazy part is that most travelers in Colombia never make it here. Getting to El Cocuy National Park takes effort…you need to acclimatize, take a long overnight bus, arrange a guide, and spend four days hiking above 4,000m. It’s not the easiest trek to get to, which is exactly why it still feels so remote and untouched. If you’re looking to get away from the crowds on famous treks like Inca Trail / Salkantay to Machu Picchu or the treks in Patogonia, this is for you. 

Despite all the incredible places I’ve visited since, this trek is still one of my favourite travel memories.

📌If you’re thinking about doing it, save these tips! 

1. You need a certified guide.  Independent trekking isn’t permitted in the park. We went with @vulturtrek and had a great experience. They handled all the logistics so we could focus on hiking.

2. The altitude is the real challenge. Every hiking day starts around 4,000m and climbs higher. Even strong hikers can struggle if they haven’t acclimatized properly. Make sure you arrive in Bogota a few days early to adapt to the altitude and do hikes like Las Moyas (see our last post for our tips on this). 

3. This is a hard trek, not because it’s technical, but because you’re spending long days hiking at extreme altitude. Expect to hike 15-20km a day with over 1000m of gain, at 4500m elevation. 

4. Overnight camping inside the park is prohibited as of recently. Instead, you’ll stay in mountain lodges near the trailheads. We stayed at Cabañas Kanwara, which made early starts easy. 

Is this trek on your bucketlist yet?

caption:
Just here for the plot 😜 How does roasting marshmallows on steam from an active volcano and following stray dogs prepare for you for the challenging Acatenango and Fuego hike you ask? 

This is part 2 of 3 in our Acatenango Guatemala series! 🇬🇹 

Follow for part 3 where I’ll show you sunrise on Acatenango 🌋

First of all I will say that Acatenango is a moderate hike - nothing extreme other than being so close to the lava itself 😅 You just need to train your ability to hike uphill and at higher altitude. 

Here are some tips on how to prepare for the intense multi day hike in Guatemala: 

1) Do the Pacaya Volcano hike to acclimate. It’s famous for emitting steam that you cook pizzas or roast marshmallows on! 

Pacaya is shorter, lower elevation that gives you a feel of volcanic terrain with loose ash and sustained uphill. It’s 5.6km, with 460m gain, a 3h drive roundtrip from Antigua, plus a 3 hour hike. Or it can be done as a multi-day where you camp on the volcano. 

⚠️comment if you want the link to this hike! 

Important to note: 
- this volcano took lives in 2010 and it led to widespread ash fall that damaged homes, crops, and the city 
- while it remains active, safety measures have been implemented such as guided tours and evacuation plans to minimize risk to hikers and impact to local residents. Please be wary and respect the unpredictability of nature. This is also why it’s important to join a tour and not go alone. 

2) Spend 2-3 days acclimating in Antigua or Lake Atitlán.

3) Practice hiking uphill with a backpack at home, and hiking for 5-6 hours. Strengthen and activate those glutes! 

4) Fuel properly the day before the trek. Eat balanced meals with carbs, protein, and electrolytes the day before. Avoid heavy fried foods or alcohol the night before

5) Hydrate more than you think you need. Start hydrating well 1–2 days before the hike, not just the morning of.

6) Hike slow and steady - it’s not a race! 

Remember: you don’t have to be an elite hiker. Many people on these tours aren’t regular hikers at all.

caption:
You asked and we delivered! Acatenango Day 1 Review + tips ⬇️ and follow for part 2!

(save + send this to your hiking buddy if Guatemala is on your bucketlist!)

Most people hike Acatenango for one reason: watching Fuego erupt. But no one really talks about what actually happens.

I also wanted to see if it was as hard as people made it out to be (spoiler: it’s not that bad 🤭).

Day 1 in a nutshell: steady uphill, navigating crowds of tourists, dusty switchbacks, hanging out at basecamp, and deciding if you have enough energy to continue to Fuego.

Extra tips:
• You can go without a guide but it’s not recommended. Weather changes fast, altitude is unpredictable, and the trail is pretty chaotic. On the positive side - it’s hard to get lost with the amount of tourists on the trail! 

• Google “acatenango 4x4 adventures” if you don’t want to hike but still want to see it!

• Porters are hired separately for up and down from the tour. People in our group were surprised when the porters left as we got to basecamp and they had to carry their own bags down 😅 

• Pack light and don’t forget you need to carry 4L of water (1L for cooking).

• Altitude affects people differently and some in our group felt it, most didn’t. Eat well, hydrate, and arrive a few days early if you can. We felt fine and never took altitude meds. 

• how to pick a tour: research for one that treats their people ethically. Look for small groups + multiple guides. Most don’t speak English so try to learn some Spanish.

$50–80usd (budget)
$90–120 (mid-range sweet spot) - we picked @lavatrails.gt 
$120–160+ (premium)

• Most tourists here aren’t regular hikers which is why they say it’s the hardest hike they’ve ever done. Even if you’re moderately fit, you’ll be okay. I’ll post more later on what you can do to prep. 

We hiked with the front guide and reached basecamp in <5hrs incl breaks (considered fast)

You need to hike faster if you want to reach Fuego for sunset. We got the prime photo spot while other groups arrived too late. 

• Bring cash for snacks, the Fuego hike (~200Q), and tips.

• Fuego might not erupt. But that’s nature for ya!

caption:
Acatenango is one of those hikes where people either overpack or pack the wrong things. You start in blazing sun, then sweat a ton as you climb steep elevation gain, then it’s freezing at camp. 

If you’re interested in seeing what it’s really like to hike Acatenango and Fuego, check out my part 1 and 2 posts on my feed and follow @ajourneyinspired for more outdoor adventure inspo! 

& If you want the full checklist I used, comment and I’ll send it over (you have to be following me or I can’t DM you!)

In addition to the packing tips in the slide: 
Here are extra packing tips ⬇️

• Your hiking pack can be the bag you brought to Guatemala. Most tour companies let you leave extra luggage at their office.

• If you hire a porter, bring a proper backpack and still pack light. 

• Bring more layers than you think you’ll need. Antigua is warm, but camp (~3,600m) gets freezing and windy. I wore a base layer, fleece, puffer, shell, gloves, and a toque on Fuego.

• Your headlamp is essential. You’ll use it for the sunrise summit and moving around camp in the dark.

• Volcanic dust gets everywhere. A buff or bandana is surprisingly helpful when the wind picks up. Same as running gaiters 

• Snacks are key. The meals are good, but the hike is long and you burn a lot of energy at altitude.

• Trekking poles help a lot on the descent. We rented one pair and shared them between us two because we couldn’t check our own on the flight (we only travelled with carry ons). 

• Bring a small battery pack. Cold temperatures drain your phone overnight.

• Bring small bills for tips. The guides and porters work incredibly hard carrying gear up the volcano.

• Hiking pants will be good, no point bringing shorts. In fact only tourists wear shorts in Latin America (locals don’t wear them!) 

• Sleeping bags came with our tour and were ready for us at th cabin. Even though they’re not cleaned often they smelled fine, but we used our own silk liners inside just in case. 

If Acatenango is on your bucket list, save this packing list so you’re actually prepared when you go!!

caption:
Rainbow Mountain without any tourists, crowds or another soul in sight?! 

We didn’t believe it could be possible to be the only ones on the iconic Rainbow Mountain (Vinicunca) in Peru given that it’s normally littered with tourists, so much that you can’t get a picture without someone in the background. 

It’s also really remote and you have to hire a tour and drive a few hours, and then hike to over 5000m above sea level. Many people take horses or ATVs because the thin air does make the hike harder! 

But…through a crazy adventure (thank goodness we came out of it alive, a story for a future post if you guys want to hear it 😂) we did manage to be the first ones here!! 

We spent a few hours of sunrise on Rainbow Mountain and Red Valley with only our friends group (even before the farmers and alpacas showed up). It was one of the most magical experiences I’ve ever had 🥹 

Have you ever been or is this hike in Peru on your bucket list? 

Follow @ajourneyinspired if you want to tips on how we got to see Rainbow Mountain without any crowds!!

The reason you hear whirring in the background is that everyone else is smart and pays for a tour guide / dune buggy up, while we tried to save every dollar by hiking. It felt like we were taking two steps backwards every time we stepped forwards 😂

This was also the first time I’d ever hiked with a bin bag instead of backpack to avoid getting sand in every crevice of my hiking gear. To this day I still haven’t gotten the sand out of my shoes. Was this worth it? Absolutely 🤩

caption:
Save this itinerary for 2 weeks in Peru!! (And hold to screenshot!)🇵🇪 

***And apologies for the typos on the days!! Edits didn’t save my edits 🥲 All the days after day 10 should be shifted down from Day 11 to 16 not 15! This is a 2 week + 2 day itinerary but you could do it in 2 weeks alone if you combine your huacachina and paracas tours into one LONG day trip (we don’t recommend it). 

Without further ado, let’s get into it! If you’re planning your first trip to Peru and feeling overwhelmed,  this the route that balances all the mountain and ocean adventures perfectly. 

We started in Cusco + the Sacred Valley to properly acclimate, then tackled Salkantay while our energy was high. Finishing the trek at Machu Picchu felt well earned and set the tone for the rest of the trip! 

After the mountains, we slowed things down with the desert + coast (Huacachina, Nazca, Paracas) and wrapped it all up in Lima eating our way through the city.

Why this itinerary works for first-timers:
• You acclimate before doing anything intense
• You save your energy for Salkantay
• You avoid rushing between regions
• You end with lower altitude + great food (your body will thank you)

Here’s our high-level route:
Cusco → Sacred Valley → Salkantay Trek → Machu Picchu → Rainbow Mountain → Lima → Huacachina → Nazca → Paracas → Lima

Would I change anything?
If you have 3–5 extra days, I’d add:
• Arequipa (2–3 days) for architecture + Colca Canyon
• Lake Titicaca (2 days) if you want a quieter, cultural stop

This trip was a mix of hard days, early mornings (2am for rainbow mountain sunrise LOL), and some of the best memories I’ve ever made and I’d recommend this flow to anyone seeing Peru for the first time.

caption:
Trail runs at 4700m above sea level hits different where the air is thinner 😮‍💨 

I’ve been getting a lot of questions about how I manage intense activity at high altitude after our group trip in Peru. 

I’m not a doctor, but a big reminder first: altitude affects everyone differently. You can be super fit and still struggle, and your experience can change day to day depending on sleep, stress, or health.

Geoff got sick right before arriving in South America and altitude hit him hard here. Later on, he hiked at high altitude again and felt totally fine.

Save these tips on how to survive high altitude hikes / runs!! ⬇️
1️⃣ Go slower than you think you need to. The effort feels 2x harder up high
2️⃣ Acclimatize properly, build elevation gradually! We did this run a couple days after we arrived with a lower elevation run the first full day 
3️⃣ Hydrate and eat more than usual with carbs and electrolytes. Altitude suppresses appetite but your body needs fuel
4️⃣ Listen to your body (headache, nausea, dizziness might mean you need to rest and descend)
5️⃣ Don’t compare yourself to anyone else, altitude is very personal!! 
6️⃣ Diamox (acetazolamide) is commonly prescribed for altitude sickness, but some people avoid it because of side effects (tingly fingers/toes, frequent washroom use, altered taste). Not for everyone! I have never taken altitude pills so I can't say how effective they are 
7️⃣ Sorojchi pills are popular in the Andes. They are herbal-based, and many travelers find them helpful for mild symptoms. I got them at the local pharmacy but never tried them either so I can’t say how well it works 
8️⃣ Beet juice / nitric oxide boosters may help with oxygen efficiency and endurance for some people. Beet powder supposedly has higher efficacy than beet crystals 
9️⃣ avoid alcohol and caffeine. Both can worsen dehydration and sleep at elevation
🔟 Build a strong aerobic base before your trip. it helps you move more efficiently once acclimatized, but it won’t replace proper acclimation

caption:
Everything I wish I knew for packing before the Salkantay trek ⤵️ 

(many of these tips and gear recs are applicable for day hiking and popular treks in Central/South America like Acatenango! 🌋)
____

This is Part 5 of my Salkantay Trek series. If you want to see what the journey was actually like, check out my previous posts :) 
____

Tbh the guided Salkantay trek feels like luxury, but without it, it’s pretty hard to logistically accomplish. The hike’s still hard at altitude, but if I had the choice I’d actually carry my own belongings without a porter. 

There’s so much I learned on this trek that you only know from experience! I’m sharing this so you can be prepared and not learn the hard way 😅 keep in mind every tour company might be slightly different! 

PACKING LIST ➡️ If you want the spreadsheet I shared with my group, COMMENT and I’ll send it to you (must be following @ajourneyinspired or I can’t DM you!) 

OTHER TIPS ⬇️

• The water provided by the cooks is filtered and safe and so much effort goes into this. I didn’t use my filter 

• Share items whenever you can like shampoo, sanitizer, sunscreen, bug spray.

• Plan for all seasons. Day 1 you’re bundled in a puffer, shell, gloves, and toque in the alpine. By the last day you’re sweating in a t-shirt in the jungle.

• pack snacks, what they give you isn’t enough 

• Your daypack can’t be too big. Machu Picchu has strict bag size limits

• Bring your own sleeping bag liner. I’d also bring my own sleeping bag next time. We actually negotiated and got all our rentals for free including hiking poles, sleeping bag, liner, and upgraded mattress. 

• Save 1 clean outfit for Aguas Calientes - you’ll want clean clothes after the hot shower at the end 

• Before the trek, your luggage is stored at a large facility. On the last day it’s a bit chaotic getting everything back into your suitcase on the street

• no one wears shorts in South America! 

• Bring change in soles for tips, snacks, bathrooms, & hot springs.

• Hiking boots were overkill for me. They asked us to bring runners too and I changed into them after day 1 

Any questions? Follow @ajourneyinspired for more adventure travel tips!!

caption:
If wild ice skating is on your bucketlist, save these unique tips! ⤵️

Skating on lakes in the Canadian Rockies is magical, but timing and conditions may matter more than the location itself and sometimes it’s just the luck of the draw!

1️⃣The best skating usually happens after lakes are fully frozen but before heavy snowfall. Some lakes show beautiful patterns but after the first snow fall they are no longer visible. Snow can insulate weak spots and hide cracks.

2️⃣ This year we’ve had abnormal amount of snow which has actually prevented the lakes from freezing properly! Lake Louise is usually ready by Christmas but it was still not ready this week when we went. 

3️⃣ Always check ice thickness (at least 10–12 cm or 4-5in of clear ice), look for signs of other skaters, and don’t assume a popular lake is safe just because it was last week. If the lake looks unvisited for days, maybe don’t go! Ice conditions can change fast

4️⃣ Daylight hours are shorter in the winter so give yourself the proper amount of time so you’re not skating in the dark 

5️⃣ Make sure to sharpen your skates before to prevent catching on bumps unnecessarily because wild can be very rugged. The ice also ruins your blades quicker so you may need to go for another sharpening soon after. 

6️⃣ Facebook groups like “Wild Ice Alberta” and “Bow Valley Wild Ice” are especially helpful for current conditions from locals. 

7️⃣ Study up on how to self rescue (ie. from YouTube) if you do fall into the water - you never know when you might need it and hypothermia can be very quick and serious! 

8️⃣Always go with a buddy and tell someone who is not with you where you are. 

9️⃣ Wear a helmet especially if you’re not familiar with skating 

🔟Always bring a shovel even if it hasn’t snowed recently. Wild ice skating is a community effort. People clear ice for each other, not just themselves, and that’s part of what makes it special.

Leave no trace: pack out anything you bring and help keep the ice clean for everyone.

Do you think Machu Picchu is really worth visiting (and hiking for many days to see)? 

Save these tips if seeing this Wonder of the World in Peru is on your bucket list! 🤍
____ 

In November I had the chance to lead a women’s only group trip to Peru and it was one of the best experiences in my life (and I would love you to join me next time!!)

I came back with sooo many tips stories to tell you including what I’ll detail below so send this to your travel buddy and keep reading! ⬇️ 

Everyone shares this iconic postcard photo, but very few people talk about how nuanced visiting Machu Picchu actually is, especially once tickets, circuits, time slots, weather, and transport are involved.

Here’s the story of what actually happened to us behind the scenes ⤵️

A few months before our trip, Kerry and I discovered our tour guide @trekwithalpaca accidentally booked us Circuit 3 for the 6-9am entry, which does not include the classic postcard viewpoint. 

Circuit 2 (the most popular circuit with the best mix of viewpoints + ruins) was completely sold out online. This was so disappointing 😭 Fortunately because we discovered this ahead before our trip, through back channels, @mapo_tapo managed to secure Circuit 2 tickets for 9-12pm later that same morning. 

The day we had been anticipating finally comes. It was rainy season and completely foggy when we entered zero visibility (see the carousel for realistic pictures!) We still went ahead and toured circuit 3B in complete fog at 6am, but all of a sudden at 8:30am the fog lifted, just in time for our Circuit 2 tour! 

Doing two tours in one morning, despite being exhausted from trekking the Salkantay, turned into the most perfect Machu Picchu day we could have asked for. Plus it was basically buy-one-get-one-free because of the tour guide’s mistake 😂 And this is why I believe everything happens for a reason ❤️
_____ 

This post is part of my “What it’s really like to hike the Salkantay Trek” series. If you’re planning Peru, hiking South America, or just dreaming right now…

caption:
If you adventure outdoors, this is for you. 👇

What we often take for granted…like the trails we hike, the lakes we swim in, the mountains we climb…exist on the traditional lands of Indigenous peoples. 

The frames I’m showing you in this video wouldn’t be possible if it weren’t for the Huu-ay-aht, Ditidaht, and Pacheedaht First Nations, who, through cooperative management with Parks Canada, continue to steward and protect the West Coast Trail so that we have access to hike it. 

Today is National Truth and Reconciliation Day and it’s not just a moment to wear an orange shirt. It’s a chance to pause, reflect, and recognize the history, resilience, and contributions of First Nations, Métis, and Inuit communities.

As people who love the outdoors, we have a responsibility to tread lightly, listen deeply, and honour the stories of the land. Appreciating its beauty is a privilege, but acknowledging its history is our responsibility.

Being an ally isn’t just about wearing orange or sharing a post. It’s about reflection and action. 

To start, we can ask ourselves:

1️⃣How has my enjoyment of this land been shaped by its colonial history?

2️⃣Do I understand whose land I’m exploring, and the legacy of that history?

3️⃣Am I listening to Indigenous voices and perspectives, or only learning from what’s convenient for me?

4️⃣How can I support and respect the communities who have stewarded this land for generations?

We can witness these stunning views and feel the freedom of being outdoors, yet still be cognizant of the truth.

How are you showing up as an ally both on the trail and in everyday life? Please share if this resonated with you🧡

I know so many of you are planning for this backpacking trip next year (permits come out in April) so I hope giving you a visual of the trail will help :)

1. This is a moderate level hike. Experienced backpackers won’t find it challenging to go all the way to Berg Lake in one day (20km+). 

However there are views on the entire way down the trail so even if you can’t / don’t want to hike all the way into Berg Lake, you don’t need to :) 

2. When booking permits, you’ll need to know how you plan on sectioning out your hike. Popular stops are Whitehorn (our halfway point for lunch) or Emperor Falls. 

Also, the reason we had to stay overnight at a rest stop was because you need to pick your permits up from the office between 8am - 4pm and we had arrived too late the day before. 

3. The hike may take longer that you anticipate because you’ll stop to take pictures too often especially at Emperor falls 😌 

4. It gets really cold here given that Mt Robson is the highest point in the Canadian Rockies - our winter sleeping bags were perfect for the end of September 

5. The campsite we hiked to was Marmot - it’s a tiny campsite and we had 2 tentpads booked but had to share 1 😅 Even though we could have stayed at Berg Lake Campsite we wanted to experience this smaller  and more peaceful one. It was worth it!

Day 2 of our Mt. Robson adventure had it all: 24km of hiking, about 6 hours of moving time (plus more for photos, snacks, and soaking up the views), fall colours, epic glaciers, and wildlife sightings! 

Save these tips if you want to hike this trail someday:

- it’s about 45km from Berg Lake Trailhead so most people do Snowbird Pass by itself as a day hike unless you’re trail running 

- Dogs are allowed on trail, but it’s a long hike with lots of elevation gain. However dogs aren’t allowed to stay overnight and backpack with you in Mt Robson so plan accordingly (some dog owners camp in Jasper and hike over)

caption:
Here’s my honest review ⬆️ and some Rainbow Mountain tips for your visit! ⬇️ (save and send this to your hiking buddy 🥾)

The classic Rainbow Mountain (aka. Vinicunca) sits at 5,036m and is one of Peru’s most iconic hikes. 

The trail itself is short but no joke thanks to the altitude. Most people take 1.5 to 2 hours up, and many opt for horses or ATVs near the top. We hiked it at sunrise, which completely changed the experience.

A few things I wish everyone knew before going:

• This isn’t the only Rainbow Mountain. If crowds aren’t your thing, look into Palcoyo instead. It’s lower elevation, less steep, and way quieter you’ll still get rainbow colours without the struggles. 

• Bring cash. You’ll need it for:
- photos with alpacas (around 4 soles)
- Red Valley entry (30 soles pp, sometimes negotiable)
- Entry to Rainbow Mountain (25 soles pp) 

• What to pack: Layers (it’s freezing early and sunny later), windproof jacket, sunscreen, hat, gloves, water, snacks, and small bills. The weather changes fast up there as you can see my friend was stuck in a snow storm! I didn’t use hiking poles and hiked it in trail runners (easy terrain). 

• Altitude tips: I didn’t feel a thing even without meds! But move slow, hydrate, eat well the days before, and listen to your body. Some people take altitude meds, some don’t. If altitude hits you hard, there’s zero shame in turning around, taking an ATV, or choosing a lower-altitude hike near Cusco instead.

• Standard group tours are around $40 pp and arrive mid-morning when it’s packed. Sunrise means hiring a private guide, which can cost $200–250 pp. Our sunrise hike ended up being around $90 pp because of a very chaotic mix-up (story for another time)… and the company no longer exists 😅 so feel free to ask me for a tour link but don’t ask me for this guide’s contact.

Was Rainbow Mountain worth it? For us, 100%, because we chose a quieter experience, respected the place, and didn’t rush it. Rainbow Mountain isn’t just a photo spot. It’s much more magical than that and a very sacred place.

Looking back, the best parts of this year weren’t the ones we planned. In fact, almost none of this was on our bingo card when we started 2025 😂

As life unfolded, we said yes to bigger goals and got more intentional about what mattered most: building community in a city that was once brand new to us. November marked one year of officially calling Vancouver home.

We ran places we once had on a “maybe someday” list, traveled far, balanced careers in finance and tech, took care of our spiritual and mental health and our friends, and worked on side projects we’re proud of (with no pitching for a five-figure content creation year!) 

But what ended up mattering most wasn’t distance, elevation, or checking things off. It was the people…the conversations on trail, shared snacks, moving through hardship together, and learning that community doesn’t just happen. To have a village, you have to make time to be the village.

What this year’s recap didn’t show were the long work weeks, red eye flights to and from Toronto, tired bodies, and the constant practice of learning when to push forward and when to pause. 

This year taught us that growth usually feels uncomfortable, that adventuring local can be just as meaningful as far away, and that rest isn’t wasted time, it’s part of sustainability in the long run. 

That’s why we want to thank the 10,000 of you who found your way here. Social media is a highlight reel, but this community is built in the unglamorous moments in between, and we’re grateful you’re here.

As we look toward 2026, we hope you choose curiosity over certainty, connection over comparison, and presence over productivity. Ask better questions and think critically about the world around you. Move at a pace that actually feels sustainable. If our posts inspire you or make you think a little differently about where you live, how you care for others, or what you’re working toward, that’s more than enough for us. 

Between the mountaintops and the valleys, thanks for being here.

caption:
Tips for packing your backpacking bag, using our West Coast Trail packing list for 4 days in late August! 

1)Line your pack with a contractor bag (even the best packs soak through after a day of rain).
2)Bring 4 pairs of wool socks, this is one thing you won’t regret doubling up on.
3)choose synthetic over down for insulation because the WCT is damp and humid.
4)we used permethrin and treated all our clothes to eliminate the need for bug spray and worrying about ticks
5)Don’t carry too much water. 1.5L was plenty, with sources almost everywhere.
6)Use what you already have. You don’t need new gear to enjoy the WCT. :) 

PACKING LIST: Save this post for reference!
Bags
- @durstongear Kakwa 55
- Dry bags: 10L for food, 5L for clothes
- Backpack liner

Tops
- Sunshirt
- @icebreakernz Hiking shirt

- @arcteryxbc Gamma tapered pants
-  shorts
- sleep leggings

Accessories
- @outdoorresearch gaiters 
- @matadorequipment lightweight towel
- @smartwool_canada socks 
- Lightweight breathable hat
- Sunglasses

Jackets

Sleep System
- @marmot Trestles Elite sleeping bag, rated to –1°C 
- @thermarest NeoAir Xherm sleep pad 
- @naturehike.canada tent (first backpacking tent we ever bought and still works fine!)

Essentials
- Water system: 1L SmartWater bottle + @hydrapak filter bag (TIP: water sources are plentiful. Don’t overpack, but note some are brackish near the ocean.) 
- 20,000 mAh battery pack
- First aid + emergency kit
- @blackdiamond headlamp
- Bear spray
- Trekking pole 
- UL camera + lens
- Inflatable pillow + silk pillowcase 
- Tarp + paracord (backup shelter)
- Toiletries 

Food
- we pre-packed per day in individual bags, then stuffed it all in a dry bag.  Bears bins can be rough so your food should survive tossing around, or be hangable if bins are full

caption:
This might be the best larch hike I’ve ever done… and you’ve likely never heard of it before. 

You’ve probably seen those instagram posts showing insane traffic jams and parking situations, and that we were not going to let that ruin the magic of fall for us 🙅‍♀️🙅🐶

So we read maps and scoured the internet and found this gem! We nearly got the entire valley of larches to ourselves and it was one of the most magical experiences we’ve ever had 🥹 

Here are some tips if you want to find your own hidden gems: 

1️⃣ Skip the hype. See which trails are trending online and then look for nearby alternatives that no one’s talking about.

2️⃣ Take the side trails. Most popular trailheads have smaller loops or connectors that are quiet, and often just as stunning.

3️⃣ Go off peak like weekdays or just before/after peak season, and you’ll almost always get them to yourself. (These pictures were actually taken on Canadian thanksgiving weekend last year so it is possible to avoid crowds during peak season!) 

4️⃣ Check the maps. Topo maps show passes, valleys, and ridges that photos don’t capture.

5️⃣ Ask locals. Hiking groups and local guides usually know the secret spots that don’t show up online.

If you want the location of this hike which was not far from Vancouver BC, Follow and comment/DM me, and I’ll send you the AllTrails link!

caption:
Here’s my honest recap of Acatenango Day 2 and all the behind-the-scenes moments you rarely see on social media!
 (save + share with your hiking buddy if hiking in Guatemala is on your bucketlist 🥾)

Day 2 in a nutshell: summit push, sunrise views, and the epic run down volcanic gravel.

Here are some extra tips:

• Small groups matter. We went with @lavatrails.gt and loved it. Our smaller group let us start a bit later, pass other hikers, and reach the top faster. It was way better than being stuck with a massive group in the cold and dark.

• Wake-up call is 4am. Bring layers, headlamps, and gloves. It’s cold, windy, and dark, but watching the sun rise over Fuego was incredible. 

• Snacks are a must because breakfast is served after the summit hike. Bring carbs for the climb.

• Even on Day 2, altitude can hit fast. Listen to your body, there’s no shame in skipping part of the summit hike if needed. Some in our group felt really sick, others were fine.

• The descent is tricky with loose volcanic gravel and steep sections. Gaiters and good grip shoes are a huge help. Trekking poles make it easier if you brought them.

And if you’re wondering if the hype is worth it… even with crowds and no eruption, Acatenango + Fuego was still one of the most epic hikes I’ve done in my life.

caption:
Did you guess our pack weight before and after backpacking the West Coast Trail? 😜

Important info + tips below ⬇️ (plus my hot take on ultralight backpacking that might ruffle some feathers…)

Pack weight check:
- Before: 33 lbs pp after evening things out
- After: 24lbs at Parks Canada’s tent in Pachena Bay, and 21lbs once we reweighed at our car (after drinking water)

This trail is no joke. Think ladders, slippery boulders, cable cars, and 75km of mud. Packing smart is what let us finish in 4 days instead of the usual 6–8.

We packed heavy on food to prep for emergencies (river ferries, tide crossings, or delays). We also hiked northbound, meaning we tackled the hardest sections first with the heaviest pack. 

Tips for keeping your backpack light:
- Aim for ~25% of your body weight

- An ultralight pack helps a lot, but here’s where i have a bone to pick…
🔥 hot take: Ultralight culture can feel like a competition, but every trip is different. UL folks love to flex their 20lb base weight, but context matters. Some trails require extras (tarp, bear bin, trowel, waste carry-outs). Different seasons means different gear. And tbh UL gear is expensive. Having the “perfect” setup is a privilege, not a standard. Use what you have. We started with an Amazon tent + Marmot sleeping bags and made it work. Our @durstongear + @rab.equipment.na packs were upgrades later. 

- You’ll probably pack more food than you need (aim for ~3500 cal/day plus emergencies). For the WCT, we packed 8 lbs of food each, tracked every calorie, and actually ate almost everything 

Extras we took + recommend:
- Gardening gloves (lifesaver for cable cars + boulders)
- Towels (to shower in creeks and wipe condensation off the tent)
- Lightweight camera
- Clean sleep clothes
- One trekking pole each
- Gaiters
- Inflatable pillow with silk pillow case (my sleep score was 100 everyday 🤭)

What we skipped:
- chairs
- tripod
- DSLR (too risky + heavy with ladders/boulders)
- down gear🪶

What I wish I skipped:
- 1L of extra water (2.5L wasn’t necessary with so many water sources)
- The tarp (rain was forecasted)

Were you surprised by any of this? 🤭

Stay tuned for our full WCT packing list next!

caption:
TIPS for trail running ⬇️ (Save this if you want to try trail running or doing a trail race!) 

We’re not experts by any means, but in the slides and caption are some great random tips that we picked up when we trained and ran Squamish 50! 🤗

1) use a big ziplock to hold everything inside your vest to keep your belongings waterproof! Even if it doesn’t rain, your sweat will seep through and make everything wet including your spare socks and bandaids (side note: make sure you have access to both of these) 🙃

2) This one was key for us: pre-measure and pre-package your race food so you don’t have to make split second decisions and delay fueling while focusing on the trail. 

We had help from our sports dietitian and can say that eating properly while running has improved our experience significantly! 

3) Have variety in what you eat! 8 hours of carbs is a lot to take in, and personally I get so tired of sugar after that 😅 That’s why we drink half of our carbs in the form of @naakbars Ultra Energy and Gatorade (to get electrolytes and sugars at the same time). 

Also, you may often hear people say fueling with candy (like nerds gummy clusters) is the best thing about trail running, but in reality, it’s not practical. 

You have to eat a whole pack of nerds clusters to even get close to your hourly carb requirement and it’s too much to carry during a race. While we do train with candy (to save money), for races, you’ll see in the slides that we carry a mix of gels, bars and other forms of sugar. 

Anyways we hope this helps shed some light into the behind the scenes of trail racing! It can be an intimidating sport to start and I always find it helpful to see what others are doing ☺️

caption:
Introducing…the most unique trail we’ve ever hiked: the West Coast Trail 😍

We put this hike off for a long time, thinking it was too touristy and not “mountain” enough, but it completely blew us away. It far exceeded our expectations and is definitely worth putting on the bucketlist!! 

📍 if you don’t know much about it, The West Coast Trail spans 75km (our watches recorded 86km) of rugged coastline in Pacific Rim National Park Reserve on Vancouver Island, BC. 

It’s often called one of the hardest and most bucket list hikes in Canada and takes 7-8 days to backpack. 

It’s incredibly unique because…

🌲 you have to climb 70+ ladders, and trek through mud bogs, cable cars, and tidal shelf crossings

🐻 Wildlife like bears, wolves, sea lions & even orcas offshore (credits to our new friend Oliver for the orca video!) 

🌊 A rare combo of rainforest + beach hiking (tide charts decide your route)

🏕️ Camping on wild beaches & catching ocean sunsets

🦀 A mid-trail Crab Shack serving fresh seafood

⚓ A trail built on history, once a lifesaving route for shipwreck survivors

✨ Walking through the traditional lands of three First Nations territories (who partner with Parks Canada and make this possible)

caption:
Join us for another storytime carousel and thank me later for these random useful tips you’ll want to save! 😉

Permit reservations open around January so it’s not too early to begin planning.

Here is our West Coast Trail on Vancouver Island (4 full day) itinerary:
🏕️ Day 1: Gordon River → Thrasher (7 km, half day) 
🏕️ Day 2: Thrasher → Bonilla (21 km)
🏕️ Day 3: Bonilla → Crab Shack (16 km)
🏕️ Day 4: Crab Shack → Michigan (21 km)
🏕️ Day 5: Michigan → Pachena (12 km) - finished by 10:30am 

TIPS: 
1) West Coast Trail app by Brett Marl offline version is a lifesaver! 

2) Know your tides. Brett’s app is pretty reliable. Missing a window can cost hours or a harder route.

3) northbound from Gordon River to Pachena is the way to go. It’s easier to ensure you can make the tides and see the sea caves at Owen point 

4) Gaiters are a must! mud and puddles are everywhere. I wouldn’t wear the gaiters with the belt that goes under your boot for the boulders though; it could cause you to slip more. 

5) everything smelly must go into bear bins. Keep backpacks in your tent due to mice. 3-person tent for 2 people is perfect.

6) Don’t pack down, everything stays damp. Polyester dries fastest.

7) your legs may burn on the ladders but focus on footing, not the height. One person at a time. 

8) bring a bandana or small towel to wipe condensation off your tent

9) I only needed 1.5L at a time since water sources are plentiful 

10) watch for bears near beaches during breakfast or dinner, they come out to snack during those times! 

11) keep your valuables close to you - our trail friend suspects that someone stole belongings at camp 

12) go at a pace you’re comfortable with! It’s a thru hike so you can spend up to 14 days per parks Canada. The longer you are on trail the more you’ll need to pack, and probably take a shower at the waterfalls. 

13) Go in without expectations and have fun!Backpacking the West Coast Trail will be one of the most memorable experiences in your life. 

Any questions? Don’t be shy to ask :)

In November, I led a women’s-only @mapo_tapo group trip with @trekwithalpaca and it was the most heart-filling trip we could’ve asked for.

Days 3–5 of the Salkantay Trek to Machu Picchu are where everything shifts…alpine terrain turns into jungle and the excitement towards seeing one of the world’s greatest wonders really starts to build.

This is Part 3 of my “What It’s Really Like to Hike the Salkantay Trek” series, covering the journey from Wayracmachay Camp to Machu Picchu, including jungle hiking, coffee farms, Llactapata ruins, and our first Machu Picchu sighting.

Since there wasn’t room to fit everything into the slides, here are a few extra tips ⬇️

1️⃣ Don’t underestimate the jungle heat! 
After days in alpine conditions, the descent into the jungle feels hot and humid. We were suddenly grateful for light wool layers, sunscreen, and bug spray. 

2️⃣ even if you’re hiking with strangers talk about tipping. Assign a group leader and Pre-arrange tips with your group so no one feels put on the spot at the end. We followed Alpaca’s tipping guidelines, but amounts are very subjective and what matters most is doing it thoughtfully and as a group.

3️⃣ You can get cash in Aguas Calientes (day 5) if you run low before you tip your guide on Day 6 (the other tips are given before that so bring enough). If you feel attached to your guides like we did, you can buy cards for them at the market in Aguas. 

4️⃣ you’ll need a pack big enough to carry your camp clothes for day 4, but small enough to enter Machu Picchu. There is a bag check at the entrance, and if your pack is too large, you’ll have to pay to store it. A 30L pack is ideal and anything bigger becomes a hassle later.

5️⃣Align expectations with your guide for Machu Picchu day. Confirm timing, logistics, and tickets before you go to sleep in Aguas Calientes so nothing catches you off guard the next morning.

And that brings us to the big question…
after all this effort will we actually get to see Machu Picchu?

caption:
Tips for Panorama Ridge / Black Tusk below ⬇️ 

Here’s the thing: most people only show the classic Panorama Ridge shot. 

But what about the 30+ km trek for 12h to get there and the risk that there may not be a view? 

We ran the whole thing in a day and want to share what it’s really like (look at my prior post for more tips). 

Here’s what you need to know: 

1) during June to mid Oct, you need a day-use pass to start at Rubble Creek (book it 2 days ahead at 7am on BC Parks).

If you can’t get one, no worries, try Cheakamus Lake parking (it’s less popular). Hike via Helm Creek is a quieter, longer alternative.

2) The trail is 30–40km with serious elevation. You should be comfy running or hiking for 8–10 hours with some climbs.

3) Pack smart: trail shoes, layers, food, filter + water (refill at streams or Garibaldi Lake), helmet if you want to summit Black Tusk, and definitely bear spray. 

Rubble Creek was recently closed for cougar activity.

4) You’ll find outhouses at Rubble Creek, Taylor Meadows, Garibaldi Lake, and Helm Creek. 

If you need to pee on trail, ensure you are at least 60m from water, and try to go on durable surfaces like rocks to not harm fragile vegetation. 

5) The trail itself is mostly smooth singletrack and alpine meadows with an easy scramble. We saw lots of beginners and tourists out there, so it’s accessible.

6) Morning fog is common but usually clears by early afternoon (ours lifted around 2pm).

7) Sunset is around 8:30pm in summer so bring a headlamp just in case you’re still on the trail after dark. 

8) The ideal time to hike is in July / Aug because snow should be melted by then. Before that the ridge may be too dangerous to ascend 

9) if you want to backpack, you can get permits at Taylor Meadows, Garibaldi Lake, or Helm Creek, popular 1–2 night options.

10) Be kind on the trail, LNT, and uphill traffic has right of way. 

Oh, and that last viewpoint was actually found on the way down when we were about to leave disappointed when the fog wouldn’t go away. Sometimes the best moments are unplanned🙃

If you’ve ever wondered what backpacking food actually looks like daily, here’s how I fueled 5 days on the West Coast Trail without carrying a crazy heavy pack!

This carousel is so value packed I had couldn’t fit it all and wrote a long caption with more tips 🤭⬇️

Here are some things that we’ve learned over the years from trial + error on the trail. 

📌Save this if you want a food guide you can actually use later!

Note:
• We used to make our own backpacking food, but lately we’ve been jamming in trips and don’t have time 😅 
• Backpacking meals are pricey so don’t feel pressured to buy $20 dried meals if it’s not in your budget.
• We’re not fancy or picky people...we eat on the go and keep things simple 
• We don’t count calories in real life, but for backpacking we do track because every ounce matters when you’re carrying it for 75km+ (Strava said 86km!). I tried my best to finish my food but I’m not perfect 🙃

⸻
Tips & what works for us:
✅ Pre-portion food by days so you don’t under/overeat
✅ 3,000–4,000 cals/day is a good baseline for intense trips like the WCT
✅ UL backpackers often aim for 1.5–2 lbs of food per day. Our total was ~8 lbs
✅ Always pack according to your needs (another reason calorie counts help)
✅ Have a daily treat to look forward to (ours was candy and pub mix)
✅ Electrolytes with real sugar are a game changer like @liquidiv
✅ Expect to have food leftover on the last day and continue to snack on those 
✅ Cold + quick breakfasts make mornings easier (RX bars ftw)
✅ Keep your day’s food in an outside pocket so you’re not digging in your pack
✅ Use a dry bag for all food to go into the bear bin/hang
✅ Check every pocket of your bag + clothes at night for scraps before bear bin time
⸻

Food ideas we love
🥯 Bagged tuna in pita
🧀 Hard cheese for the first few days (parm + pecorino hold up well)
🥩 Good quality meat sticks (skip the overly salty ones)
🍜Chinese egg noodles are lighter than ramen
⸻
What didn’t work for us
🚫 warm breakfasts bc we don’t have time 
🚫 Forgetting to hydrate. water is fuel too!
⸻

Lmk if this was helpful and ask if you have any questions!

caption:
Every Canadian Thanksgiving long weekend (mid Oct), Geoff and I make a point to visit someplace new that still has fall colours. 

You’d think that most of them will have faded by then but when we had limited vacation time, we turned it into a challenge 😏 

So, we wanted to share some of our favourite places in case you haven’t made plans yet or haven’t had the chance to hike for the fall colours 💛

📌Save this post for your fall trip inspiration!

Here are some tips and hike locations ⬇️DM me if you want any of the specific hike locations in the carousel. 

🍁North Cascades, Washington
- Some tips: colour in higher elevations (ie. Washington Pass, Maple Pass Loop) usually peak in late September but Lower valleys (Diablo Lake, Newhalem area) extend into early October.
- The larches are usually the the highlight of this area and they might come late this year due to the unseasonably warm start of fall we’ve gotten! 

🍁 Killarney, Ontario (Georgian Bay area)
- Ontario is famous for its maples/birches. There is an online colour tracker!
- make sure you hike The Crack trail and see the old La Cloche Mountains (did you know Ontario has mountains?! 😱) 
- also make sure you spend some time in Muskoka and Alogonquin areas. Ontario falls hold such a special place in my heart 

🍁 Chéticamp, Nova Scotia (Cape Breton Highlands)
- The Cabot Trail is famous for its rolling red/orange hills.
- Oct 5-15 is usually the peak window. Colours come later than Ontario because the Atlantic Ocean moderates the climate

🍁 Canadian Rockies (Banff, Jasper, Yoho)
- ok I snuck this one in but the Rockies might have just hit their peak in mid to late September. They don’t get huge displays of maples but the larches are really special. We even got to see them at Berg Lake!
- Sept 15-25 is usually prime in Banff and Lake Louise (Larch Valley, Sentinel Pass). If you missed these higher elevation areas, visit lower valleys 

🍁 Adirondacks, New York
- High Peaks Wilderness (Lake Placid, Keene Valley) peaks earlier but lower areas (Lake George, Saranac Lake) hold colour into Oct.

caption:
Part 1 | The reality of backpacking adventures & the Berg Lake trip recap you’ve all been asking for😄

After work, we drove 8 hours straight to the BC Alberta border to get ready for a 20km hike into Mt Robson backcountry the next day. 

Instead of paying for a campsite inside the park, we overnighted at a rest stop that my brother’s gf found. It was free, had clean heated washrooms, running water, Wi-Fi, and surprisingly safe. 

We’re certainly living proof that you don’t need a fancy setup to go car camping! We just rolled out our backpacking gear (@thermarest @mec) in our trusty @toyotacanada matrix, the best adventure car!

(DM me for the📍location if you’re planning on going to Berg Lake too)

Some may frown at how unglamorous sleeping in our trunk is, but it’s very comfy and $30 to park our car for 5 hours wasn’t worth it 😅 

Here are tips for staying at free rest stops / overnight spots when you’re travelling in the Rockies! ⤵️

(save for trip planning)

1️⃣ Look for truck stops and highway rest areas. 
- on Google Maps search “rest area,” “truck stop,” or “highway pullout” along your route
- Many are free to park overnight (check signage). 
- Arrive late and leave early. 
- Bring ear plugs or be able to sleep to the sound  of rumbling semi truck generators!
- Avoid blocking other vehicles, especially truckers who are just trying to get some rest before going to work 
- Pack out all trash, and don’t make fires
- bring water or a filter at minimum, the tap water might not be potable

2️⃣Use Apps & Websites
- iOverlander is a user-submitted database of campsites, rest stops and legal parking overnight
- AllStays / Park4Night shows truck stops, parking lots, rest areas, and free camping options.
- Walmart parking lots are free and easy if you’re within city limits 
- Prioritize well-lit, busy areas for safety.

caption:
Part 2️⃣ - the good ✅, the bad 👎🏻, and the ugly😈 … of running 160kms with our friends for the Sinister 7 relay race 😛 

The first half of Sinister 7 (legs 1-4 out of 7, 93km out of 160 total) tested our team with extreme heat, technical climbs/descents and other challenges. 

We wanted to show you some of the trials and tribulations Geoff and I faced and how our team did. There’s not enough space to write about it all so you’ll have to watch the whole video 😆

😈 So the bad news first… Geoff had a freak accident and sprained his ankle badly on a trail run the same week of the race. It was terribly bruised and a ligament was likely & partially torn. 

✅ the good: Geoff felt great despite his injury, so after seeing his physio and considering this is not our main race of the summer (we still have an ultra coming up), he switched race legs with me. He ended up running a very technical downhill which still isn’t good for his foot but at least it was 10km shorter and he absolutely crushed it! 

✅ I ran Geoff’s leg (leg 4, 26km up and down a steep mountain) which was much more than I was mentally prepared for, so to be honest I was quite nervous. However, I still finished 1 hour ahead of schedule and it got to see some of the most stunning scenery. 

😈 the bad - my leg 4 (rated 5/7 difficulty) was full of tricks. I had to climb a barb wired fence but nope, the cuts and bruises you see in the video are not from that. I managed to run the steep downhills but fell on flat ground, and blood was streaming down my leg for 15kms 🤣 The trail was also poorly marked so many runners including me got lost despite having a map on my watch. 

👎🏻 Also, I ran most of leg 4 solo. I was quite worried that I would by hunted by a bear / cougar. Later we found out that runners did encounter an angry hissing cougar and bear spray was deployed! 

✅ Altogether our team shaved off 3 hrs from our estimates in the first half of the race. 

Our leg 5 runner set off running into the night … stay tuned to see how that goes 👀

caption:
Definitely a bucketlist hike for when you’re visiting Vancouver BC Canada!! 🇨🇦 🏔️

If you don’t live under a rock, I bet you’ve heard of 📍Panorama Ridge in Garibaldi Provincial Park 🤭 

Sure it is over-popularized so you’re probably wondering, do we think it’s worth it? 

Well, we have been very privileged to see incredible places, but yes Panorama Ridge still one of our favourite hikes and is one of the few extremely busy trails that I recommend! 

Here are some tips for hiking Panorama Ridge: 

1. The trail itself not as hard as people make it out to be, but getting a day use @yourbcparks permit is what is challenging 😅 You must book the day pass 2 days in advance of your desired date, or get a backpacking permit. 

2. It is also confusing but there are two main approaches - Rubble Creek Parking (the most popular option) and Cheakamus (less busy). 

Even if you do have a pass, arrive early, as people who bypass the system by getting there before park rangers start checking around 7am could have taken up a parking spot from those who got passes. 

I couldn’t get a pass but I posted on AllTrails comments and a kind stranger gave me his!! 

3. The Panorama Ridge trail is about 30km with 1700m of elevation gain, and we tacked on Black Tusk (up to the chimney) for a total of 34km and 2100m of gain. 

To get to the ridge, people usually go backpacking overnight or spend a long 11-13 hour day hiking. But if you’re short on time like us, the trail is incredibly smooth and perfect for a run!! We completed it in 6 hours, it’s very doable and we had energy left for a party in Vancouver after 🥳 

I’ll post a vlog soon so you can see the behind the scenes, so follow along @ajourneyinspired!

Part 3 of running 160km through the mountains with friends | Sinister 7 Relay race recap…!!🤠

A continuation from part 2…

By this point we had run 93km and I passed the chip to Bailin at golden hour, hoping she’d get most of her run in before dark. 

What actually happened?

She blazed through the leg 2 hours faster than expected, including a trail 💩💨, and a ninth grader helping pace her through the dark.

With no cell service, we were trying to catch some sleep in the car while she waited alone at the transition area at midnight. 

Thankfully, her husband Connor, who seems to have a sixth sense for these things, found her in the dark and already took off running the hardest leg of the race.

His leg was 32km with cougars, creek crossings, a crazy mountain climb and descent in total darkness. 

He came back looking like he had seen things no ER doctor should ever see.☠️

Then Hugh, our last runner, took off. He’d been waiting 21 hours for his moment.

He flew down the trail and beating 20 runners on the final leg, increasing our ranking significantly!! 

We finished 160km in 22 hours. Most of them were first-time trail racers, and we still ended up in the top 15%.

This race was brutal but it also proved how tough we were. Whatever doesn’t break you makes you stronger right? 🤪

caption:
Save this and follow for Part 2! I have sooo much to tell you about what it’s actually like to hike the Salkantay Trek to Machu Picchu in Peru (using a big photo dump from my phone!) 

In November, I led a women’s-only @mapo_tapo group trip with @trekwithalpaca and it was the most heart-filling trip we could’ve asked for.

This is Part 1 of my “What It’s Really Like to Hike the Salkantay Trek” series, covering the planning, orientation, and the pre-trek journey to basecamp.

Since there was way too much to fit into the slides, here are more tips👇 (save for your bucket list trip planning!)

1️⃣ A guided group tour makes the multi day hike much more accessible

Yes, you can hike the Salkantay Trek alone but guided tours take care of all permits, logistics, transportation, meals, camping, and allow you to actually enjoy the experience instead of managing details. Plus the group camaraderie on trail and the things the guide will teach you are so important!

2️⃣ Don’t trust the weather forecast in the Andes

Peru weather forecasts LIE 😅 We trekked in rainy season (Nov 11-16) and got perfect weather when storms were promised every day! 

Mountain weather changes by the hour so pack layers (and extra garbage bags) and go with an open mind. 

3️⃣ About altitude sickness (the biggest question I get!) … No one on our group trip got sick, and we’re soo grateful 🙌

My personal tips:
• Pre-trip: train your cardio 
• In Cusco: arrive early, hydrate, avoid alcohol + caffeine
• On the trail: hike slow, sip water constantly, breathe
• Coca candies help!
I didn’t take Diamox but the other girls did and felt tingly limbs. I just packed Sorochi Pills (purchased OTC in Cusco) as a natural backup but no one used them

4️⃣ Give yourself more vacation than you think
The 5-day Salkantay trek is actually an 11-day commitment once you include flights + acclimation time. Our trip totalled 19 days

5️⃣ Pack light but warm, especially on the first two days of the trip. Nights in Soraypampa drop below freezing even when days are warm.

Any questions? Was the hike to Machu Picchu on your bucket list or is it now? 😍

Follow @ajourneyinspired for part 2 with more Salkantay Trek tips!

caption:
Week 8 run challenge - let’s run and chat about a hot take 🔥🙊
_____ Come run 32km with us to touch the ocean while we train for #Squamish50 and drop some truth about this running culture that’s going around right now. ☠️ 

And follow our training journey at @ajourneyinspired to see what our next training challenge will be! 😄 
_____ 
Here it goes…

There’s this trend of glamorizing “winging it” or rawdogging races (with NO physical prep). 

Sure, it’s possible to pull off a half marathon with minimal prep especially if you’re active. But those who don’t prep at all? Just because you can doesn’t mean you should - it’s not a flex 😅

It’s actually risky for full marathons and ultras and that’s not just our opinion.

📌 Why does training matter? 

- It lowers injury risk: 24% of half marathoners report race injuries, compared to 30% for fulls. Undertraining is a big factor (and running through injury will cause even more problems!) 

- Physical wear & tear: running is taxing on muscles, cells, and immunity, and some runners get permanently injured.

- Mental resilience: Training builds quiet grit that carries over to life off the trails

- Better race experience: Instead of surviving, you actually enjoy the moment

- it can be fun, make challenges for yourself! we still can’t believe our dog counting run video went kinda viral (have you seen it?) 

And can we talk about undertraining and underfueling? It’s a big issue, especially for women. Running 50k on vibes alone is not it. (But maybe that’s a story for another time…)

We’re not “training too much”, we’re just not hiding it. 
 Because the training is the journey. It’s the commitment to yourself and those around you. Runners gain respect for the time they put in training for things. 

What are your thoughts on this new trend of “not training and winging a half marathon”?

caption:
Part 1️⃣ | When your friends are as delusional as you are, you end up signing up for one of Canada’s most iconic and toughest trail ultras to hang out on the weekend 😈

And if you’re wondering what this hangout consisted of, we’re attempting to run 161km (100 miles) with 6,700m (21,900ft) of elevation gain and only 30 hours to finish.

Sinister 7 is known for its relentless climbs, river crossings, unpredictable mountain weather, running through the night, wildlife danger, and deadly heat. 

Some people run it solo (major respect 🫡 ) and less than 30% of them finish, but we ran it as a 7-person relay team, because in my opinion running is a fun sport meant to be enjoyed together, and sharing the chaos makes it way better. 

On day 1, this is what we got up to behind the scenes:  
🚗 Driving from Edmonton/Calgary through Crowsnest Pass + Frank Slide (some teammates flew in from Vancouver and Seattle) 
⛺️ Camping with hundreds of other runners (because a good sleep and stretching pre race does not exist in trail running) 
🍝carb loading as starting tomorrow we’re surviving on gels and candy 
📈 Planning handoffs, pacing, and sleep schedules with no cell service and a shared Google Doc 
🫣 Nervous laughter, questionable elevation charts, and pretending we weren’t all in over our heads

caption:
Have you been to these iconic places in Canada?🇨🇦👇 

It’s Canada Day and we wanted to share some of our favourite spots in the country, but wait - we need to have an important conversation.

We’ve always felt proud to be Canadian. Growing up, we learned about our vast landscapes, our freedoms, our kindness. There’s so much to be grateful for.

But the more we time we spend exploring this land, the more we want to talk about a deeper story.

Canada didn’t start in 1867. This land has been home to Indigenous Peoples for thousands of years.

Nations with rich languages, vibrant cultures, and deep-rooted relationships to the land were here long before it was renamed and reshaped by colonization.

We did learn about this in school. Residential schools, broken treaties, cultural erasure. But sometimes we learn things too early to understand their weight, and sometimes, it’s just easier to forget what makes us uncomfortable.

So this Canada Day, let’s reflect, remember, and ask better questions.

If we say we love this country, we also have to love the full truth of it, not just the parts that make us feel proud.

To truly call this land home means recognizing the history, respecting the people who have always cared for it, and committing to being responsible stewards ourselves.

So let’s start here: native-land.ca

That’s why we pre-test all routes to ensure they’re safe, scenic, and doable for all levels. Safety is non-negotiable when leading groups in variable spring weather. 

Another big factor was keeping the route within Vancouver’s North Shore for easy free access, because logistics matter when you bring a group together. We skipped other trail options that didn’t check all our boxes (too snowy / high avi danger or not enough workout). 

We try to take care of our people.  Now you know that a lot of work goes on behind the scenes to put on events ☺️

One more note: Hypothermia is a real risk even in “mild” weather. Sweat too much, stop moving, or get caught in wet snow and cold wind and your body temp can drop fast.

Our prevention tips 👉 Pack dry layers, gloves, a lightweight jacket, emergency blanket, and keep moving once sweaty!

Part 3 - Our car got hit on the way to run club and that kind of sums up the week 😂

But instead of scrapping the run, we showed up anyway and ended up having one of the most fun training weeks so far. 

While this was only week 2 of officially starting training for one of the toughest 50k races in Canada, we’ve been road running consistently for a couple years. Naturally it can get monotonous, especially when you’re so busy with life and running is just another thing on the to do list. 

And when people ask, how do you ALWAYS enjoy running? The answer is, we don’t 😅 

At some point you’ll realize it’s not about pushing harder, but it’s about making your brain stronger.  And what it takes is pressing reset on your brain. There’s actually a term for that called “pattern interrupt”, where small changes in routine help you enjoy the process and find that spark again ✨

Here’s what we did and some ideas for you to switch things up and make running feel fun: 
1️⃣We ran with friends at a new run club (s/o to @Alo) because running is way more fun when it’s social 

Ps. If you’re looking for a run club to join in Vancouver there are tons! check out www.runclubs.ca/vancouver

2️⃣We changed our route and turned a dinner invite into a destination run with an ice cream stop on the way (instead of commuting in a car, try “runmuting” this week!) 

3️⃣Finally started seeing our friend and new sports nutritionist @sandrakilmartin @nosweatnutrition and started taking fueling more seriously (carbs are your friend)! 

4️⃣ We mixed in hiking, it counts as cross training!  That’s in addition to our strength sessions.

It wasn’t our biggest mileage week, but it reminded us that discipline doesn’t always mean grinding. It can also mean reworking the routine so you can keep showing up.

And honestly putting ourselves out here and sharing our weekly diary is kind of
vulnerable but if it’s relatable and can even help one person, then this will all be worth it!

Nope, it’s not even backpacking long distances on active volcanoes or jumping out of planes… but somehow, this might be the hardest thing yet.

This summer, we’re training for our first ultramarathon! Not just any 50K, but one of the hardest in the country.

We’ve always been about chasing big adventures and testing our limits, so of course, we had to take on something that scares us. It’s not even the craziest race (maybe someday we’ll tackle a 100k+) but remember don’t compare because you never know where people are in their journey and comparison is the thief of joy. 

But honestly, what’s even scarier than running this race is sharing the journey online. 🫣 Why are we doing this series then? caption:
We thought we were just adopting a dog, but it turns out, we found an adventure buddy we can’t live without 🥺 

Hear us out…

We didn’t know what we were getting into with Asher. They told us he’d be a 30lb medium-sized beagle. He turned out to be none of the above and somehow exactly what we needed.

He’s hiked mountains, traveled on planes, brought smiles to millions of people online, made friends out of strangers, and filled our lives with so much unexpected joy. We thought we were saving him, but actually, he saved us.

We often hear this idea that rescue dogs are all damaged. And yes, some have survived unthinkable things. But many are born into foster homes and raised with love and care. Others are rehomed by heartbroken families due to life changes.  The dogs who have known pain are often the most loving, intuitive, and grateful souls you’ll ever meet. They deserve a beautiful future just as much as any dog.

If you think you’re not ready to welcome a pup into your life, we weren’t sure we were completely ready either. We took rescue dogs on day trips while traveling, volunteered, and fostered. If adoption isn’t in the cards right now, you can still be part of an animal’s beautiful journey. 

This said, let me just set things straight - you’ll never be ready. We’re especially not ready for the day we’ll have to learn to live without him 🥺💔

If your dog came into your life in another way? That’s beautiful too. Every dog brings love. This is just the story of how ours found us.

POV: rich because we found you 🥹 

A few weeks ago, we were so lucky to be able to hike with some of the sweetest souls who found each other on Instagram. 

Many laughs were shared, new friends and memories were made, and numerous mango slices were eaten 😂🥭

Vancouver is notorious for being one of the loneliest cities in Canada, so it’s always been on @tellez_g’s and my hearts to change that narrative. Now we feel so blessed to be able to do that, one hike at a time! 

At 8am we gathered at Tunnel Bluffs (you probably saw my previous reel of us testing out the original planned routes, and if you wondered which we chose, the answer’s none of the above) 🙃 Spring hiking conditions 1000m+ in snow just aren’t pleasant for such a big gathering so we had to make the call to change the trail. 

This group hike, we got treated with special gifts from @wildandwilly (beautiful iron-on / Velcro Vancouver patches) and a pick-me-up from @guruenergydrink for the early morning start. 

The weather was absolutely perfect and spirits were so high! We hiked until 12pm and then headed to a pub in West Vancouver for a post-hike hang. 

If you want to come on our next group hike, follow 👉@tellez_g and @ajourneyinspired, and join my channel “Inspired Adventurers”👈 to be the first to know! 

Can’t wait to see you at the next one! Are you in?
